claim: Recombinant CAF-1 assembles nucleosomes in vitro in the absence of the replication machinery or other nuclear proteins.
source: Whether recombinant CAF-1 assembles nucleosomes in vitro in absence of the replication machinery or other nuclear proteins remains an open question (Gaillard et al., 1996; Kadyrova et al., 2013; Kaufman et al., 1995; Smith and Stillman, 1991), which we set out to resolve in a purified in vitro system.
evidence: The manuscript describes experiments demonstrating nucleosome assembly by recombinant CAF-1 in a purified system, as shown in Figure 1.

claim: tCAF-1 is sufficient for nucleosome assembly in vitro.
source: These experiments demonstrate that tCAF-1 and FL CAF-1 are both active and efficient nucleosome assembly factors in absence of other nuclear proteins.
evidence: Demonstrated through NAQ assay results shown in Figure 1, where tCAF-1 produces nucleosomal DNA fragments.

claim: The N-terminal portion of Cac1 is not required for nucleosome assembly activity.
source: Our results also indicate that the N-terminal portion of Cac1, which in vivo is associated with PCNA, is not required for the nucleosome assembly activity, and that tCAF-1 contains all the requisite components for histone deposition.
evidence: Supported by comparison of FL CAF-1 and tCAF-1 activities in Figure 1.

claim: Nucleosome assembly activity increases in a CAF-1 dose dependent manner and reaches its maximum at a two-fold excess of CAF-1 complex per (H3-H4)2 tetramer.
source: Nucleosome assembly activity increases in a CAF-1 dose dependent manner, and reaches its maximum at a two-fold excess of CAF-1 complex per (H3-H4)2 tetramer (Figure 1c).
evidence: Quantitative data from NAQ assay shown in Figure 1c demonstrates dose-dependent activity.

claim: The primary role of CAF-1 is to promote the formation of an ordered (H3-H4)2•DNA complex, the tetrasome.
source: it appears that the primary role of CAF-1 is to promote the formation of an ordered (H3-H4)2•DNA complex, the tetrasome, as noted previously (Smith and Stillman, 1991).
evidence: Based on observations that H2A-H2B can spontaneously associate with tetrasomes and CAF-1 has lower affinity for H2A-H2B compared to H3-H4.

claim: Each CAF-1 complex has a single binding site for one H3-H4 dimer, and CAF-bound H3-H4 is still able to tetramerize.
source: Altogether, these experiments indicate that each CAF-1 complex has a single binding site for one H3-H4 dimer, and that CAF-bound H3-H4 is still able to tetramerize, either with or without its own bound CAF-1 complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: Supported by multiple biophysical techniques including SV-AUC, Job plot, and SEC-MALS experiments.

claim: The four-helix bundle formed by two H3 molecules in the (H3-H4)2 tetramer is important for CAF-1 complex formation.
source: This suggests that the four-helix bundle formed by two H3 molecules in the (H3-H4)2 tetramer is important for this complex formation and perhaps the only point of contact between the two CAF-1 moieties.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that complexes are stable with XL(H3-H4)2 but not with WTH3-H4.

claim: CAF-1 binding to H3-H4 induces protection from exchange of an extended area on both WT and DMH3-H4.
source: CAF-1 binding to H3-H4 induces protection from exchange of an extended area on both WT and DMH3-H4, as opposed to a distinct region of protection.
evidence: Demonstrated through HX-MS experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: CAF-1 binding to histones elicits a global conformational effect.
source: This suggests that CAF-1 binding to histones elicits a global conformational effect, which was also observed for other chaperone-histone complexes (D'Arcy et al., 2013; DeNizio et al., 2014) (Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Supported by HX-MS data and comparison with published studies on other chaperones.

claim: The H3 region mediating H3-H4 tetramerization through a four-helix bundle (α3; aa 111–126) shows no significant changes in HX upon CAF-1 binding.
source: Importantly, no significant changes in HX were detected in the H3 region mediating H3-H4 tetramerization through a four-helix bundle (α3; aa 111–126) (Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 2a), confirming our interpretation that this region is exposed and available for tetramer formation in the CAF-1•H3-H4 complex.
evidence: HX-MS data shown in Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: CAF-1 binds to one H3-H4 dimer that results in its overall stabilization and permits tetramerization in its CAF-1 bound form.
source: Together, these data indicate that CAF-1 binds to one H3-H4 dimer that results in its overall stabilization, and that permits tetramerization in its CAF-1 bound form.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experiments including HX-MS, SV-AUC, and binding studies.

claim: The C-terminal Cac1 WHD is a DNA binding domain.
source: In particular, we noticed that the C-terminal Cac1 WHD, recently identified as a DNA binding domain (Zhang et al., 2016), showed deprotection upon histone binding in the HX-MS analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c), also seen when FL CAF-1 was used (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from published work and confirmed by HX-MS data.

claim: tCAF-1 does not bind DNA in absence of histones, despite containing a functional WHD domain.
source: Interestingly, tCAF-1 does not bind DNA in absence of histones, despite containing a functional WHD domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b and below).
evidence: Demonstrated through EMSA experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: In absence of histones, the WHD may be inhibited by an intramolecular interaction with the acidic region on Cac1.
source: This indicates that in absence of histones the WHD may be inhibited by an intramolecular interaction with the acidic region on Cac1, a component of the histone binding module (Liu et al., 2016) together with Cac2 (Mattiroli et al., 2017) (histone binding module is referred to as HBM, Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Inferred from experiments with mutant tCAF-1 complexes shown in Figure 3a-b.

claim: The Cac1 acidic domain engages in an inhibitory intramolecular interaction with the WHD, thereby masking its DNA binding capacity.
source: Together, these data suggest that the Cac1 acidic domain engages in an inhibitory intramolecular interaction with the WHD, thereby masking its DNA binding capacity.
evidence: Supported by competition experiments and cross-linking data shown in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: H3-H4 binding releases the DNA binding activity of tCAF-1.
source: To directly test if H3-H4 binding can unmask the DNA binding activity of the WHD, we established a gel-based DNA binding assay with tCAF-1 and histones.
evidence: Demonstrated through EMSA experiments shown in Figure 3d.

claim: H3-H4 triggers DNA binding by the WHD, by releasing it from an inhibitory intramolecular interaction with the histone binding region.
source: These data strongly suggest that H3-H4 triggers DNA binding by the WHD, by releasing it from an inhibitory intramolecular interaction with the histone binding region.
evidence: Supported by experiments with WHD mutants shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Histone tetramerization is not required for the formation of the tCAF-1•H3-H4•18DNA ternary intermediate.
source: As 18DNA can interact with XL(H3-H4)2 (Figure 4b, lane 4, demonstrated by disappearance of the free DNA band into the well), this strongly suggests that two CAF-1 moieties remain bound to the XL(H3-H4)2 tetramer, otherwise the exposed H3-H4 dimer in the constitutive tetramer XL(H3-H4)2 would remain free to mediate DNA binding even with a complex with a mutated WHD.
evidence: Demonstrated through EMSA experiments with DMH3-H4 shown in Figure 4a.

claim: 18DNA promotes the association of two tCAF-1•WTH3-H4 moieties.
source: Because the tCAF-1•WTH3-H4•18DNA and the tCAF-1•DMH3-H4•18DNA complexes migrate similarly to the complex formed with XL(H3-H4)2, which we know contains two tCAF-1 moieties (Figure 2b–c), and considerably slower than the tCAF-1•WTH3-H4 complexes without DNA (Figure 4b, lane 5–9, 488-H3-H4 red signal), we postulated that 18DNA promotes the association of two tCAF-1•WTH3-H4 moieties, and in this assembly histone tetramerization is not a requirement for complex formation.
evidence: Inferred from EMSA migration patterns and comparison with XL(H3-H4)2 complexes.

claim: Titrating 18DNA into a FL CAF-1•WTH3-H4 complex strongly promotes the formation of a discrete high molecular weight assembly.
source: Strikingly, titrating 18DNA into a FL CAF-1•WTH3-H4 complex strongly promoted the formation of a discrete high molecular weight assembly, which did not accumulate when the histones were omitted or when the Cac1 WHD was mutated (Figure 4d – Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Demonstrated through in solution cross-linking experiments shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The high molecular weight assembly formed by FL CAF-1•WTH3-H4 with 18DNA has a molar mass consistent with (CAF-1)2•(H3-H4)2•18DNA.
source: By analyzing these reactions through SEC-MALS, we confirmed that this species has a molar mass consistent with the assembly of (CAF-1)2•(H3-H4)2•18DNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Titrating 18DNA into H3-H4 in absence of CAF-1 does not significantly stimulate the formation of (H3-H4)2 tetramer.
source: Importantly, titrating 18DNA into H3-H4 in absence of CAF-1 did not significantly stimulate the formation of (H3-H4)2 tetramer, confirming that the association of two H3-H4 dimers under these conditions requires the presence of the CAF-1 chaperone (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Control experiment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Two FL CAF-1 complexes associate on 18DNA via their WHD domains when bound to histones.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that two FL CAF-1 complexes associate on a 18DNA via their WHD domains, but only do so when bound to histones.
evidence: Conclusion from cross-linking and SEC-MALS experiments shown in Figure 4d-e.

claim: Two Cac1 WHDs cooperatively bind DNA.
source: SEC-MALS experiments demonstrate that this species contains two WHD domains, and that the binding of two WHDs to a 18DNA is preferred even at a 1:1 WHD to DNA stoichiometry (Figure 4f).
evidence: SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 4f demonstrates 2:1 WHD:DNA stoichiometry.

claim: The Cac1 WHD elutes as a monomer on SEC-MALS in absence of DNA.
source: Importantly, the Cac1 WHD elutes as a monomer on SEC-MALS in absence of DNA (Liu et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016) (Figure 4f).
evidence: SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 4f and cited from published work.

claim: The interaction between DNA and the WHD is triggered by histone binding to CAF-1 and promotes the juxtaposition of two CAF-1 complexes, each pre-loaded with an H3-H4 dimer.
source: Overall, our data support a model in which the interaction between DNA and the WHD is triggered by histone binding to CAF-1, and this promotes the juxtaposition of two CAF-1 complexes, each pre-loaded with an H3-H4 dimer.
evidence: Summary conclusion from multiple experiments including EMSA, cross-linking, and SEC-MALS.

claim: The DNA-mediated association of two histone-bound CAF-1 complexes may promote the formation of the (H3-H4)2 tetramer on DNA.
source: Thus, the DNA-mediated association of two histone-bound CAF-1 complexes may promote the formation of the (H3-H4)2 tetramer on DNA.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on experimental observations.

claim: After the initial interaction via the Cac1 WHD, the formation of the ternary intermediate becomes dependent on the assembly of the (H3-H4)2 tetramer with DNA of increasing length.
source: Hence, after the initial interaction via the Cac1 WHD, the formation of the ternary intermediate becomes dependent on the assembly of the (H3-H4)2 tetramer with DNA of increasing length.
evidence: Demonstrated through experiments with 33DNA showing requirement for tetramerization (Figure 5b).

claim: Histone tetramerization is required for the formation of the ternary complex with 33DNA.
source: Strikingly, the ternary complex containing 33DNA could not be stabilized with the constitutively dimeric DMH3-H4 (Figure 5b). This is surprising, as this histone mutant is sufficient to activate DNA binding by the WHD, as seen with the 18DNA (Figure 4a). These results demonstrate that histone tetramerization is required in this context.
evidence: EMSA experiments shown in Figure 5b demonstrate inability of DMH3-H4 to form complex with 33DNA.

claim: DNA of sufficient length partially destabilizes the CAF-1•histone interaction.
source: Moreover, in cross-linking experiments with FL CAF-1 we noticed a similar trend, wherein the formation of a (FL CAF-1)2•XL(H3-H4)2•DNA complex was disfavored with 33DNA (Figure 5d, lane 5 - Figure 5—figure supplement 1c). These observations support the idea that DNA of sufficient length partially destabilizes the CAF-1•histone interaction.
evidence: Cross-linking and SEC-MALS experiments shown in Figure 5d and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: With 79 bp DNA, no intermediate could be formed and only the final assembly products, i.e. (H3-H4)2•DNA complexes, are detected.
source: Indeed, with a longer DNA (79 bp, 79DNA), suitable for complete tetramer wrapping, no intermediate could be formed and only the final assembly products, i.e. (H3-H4)2•DNA complexes, are detected (Figure 5—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: EMSA experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1d.

claim: H3-H4 dimer interaction with the CAF-1 complex releases and activates the Cac1 WHD to allow its interaction with DNA.
source: Overall, our data point to a model for CAF-1-mediated tetrasome formation in which H3-H4 dimer interaction with the CAF-1 complex releases and activates the Cac1 WHD to allow its interaction with DNA (Figure 6a).
evidence: Summary of mechanism based on multiple experiments, illustrated in Figure 6a.

claim: DNA interaction promotes the association of two histone-bound CAF-1 complexes via cooperative DNA binding of the Cac1 WHDs.
source: This interaction promotes the association of two histone-bound CAF-1 complexes, via cooperative DNA binding of the Cac1 WHDs (Figure 6b).
evidence: Mechanism illustrated in Figure 6b, supported by experimental data.

claim: The integrity of DNA binding by the WHD is a pre-requisite for tetrasome formation and nucleosome assembly.
source: Our model predicts that the integrity of DNA binding by the WHD is a pre-requisite for tetrasome formation and hence nucleosome assembly.
evidence: Tested through NAQ assay with WHD mutants shown in Figure 7a.

claim: tCAF-1 complexes with a mutated or deleted WHD exhibit reduced nucleosome assembly activity.
source: Indeed, in the NAQ assay, tCAF-1 complexes with a mutated or deleted WHD exhibit reduced nucleosome assembly activity (blue bars in Figure 7a).
evidence: Quantitative NAQ assay data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: WHD mutant complexes preferentially form subnucleosomal particles with protected DNA fragments around 100 bp rather than 126–160 bp.
source: Notably, with these mutant tCAF-1 complexes we also observed a dose-dependent increase in protected DNA fragments around 100 bp rather than the 126–160 bp fragments observed with tCAF-1 and wild type CAF-1, indicative of the formation of subnucleosomal particles (Figure 7b).
evidence: NAQ assay data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Abrogating WHD-dependent DNA binding or preventing H3-H4 tetramerization result in the same deposition product in vitro: a single H3-H4 dimer bound to DNA.
source: This finding indicates that either abrogating WHD-dependent DNA binding, or preventing H3-H4 tetramerization, result in the same deposition product in vitro, a single H3-H4 dimer bound to DNA.
evidence: Demonstrated through tetrasome assembly assays shown in Figure 7c.

claim: The WHD domain is important for Cac1 functions in the context of full-length Cac1 in vivo.
source: While WT Cac1 protein could completely rescue the growth phenotype on FOA plates, FL Cac1 WHD mutants did not, reflected by delayed growth (Figure 7d and Figure 7—figure supplement 1b). This indicates that the WHD domain is indeed important for Cac1 functions in the context of full-length Cac1 in vivo, in agreement with previous work (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: Yeast heterochromatin maintenance assay shown in Figure 7d.

claim: Okazaki fragments purified from yeast strains carrying mutations or deletions in the Cac1 WHD domain do not exhibit the periodicity characteristic of a proficient replication-coupled nucleosome assembly pathway.
source: Strikingly, Okazaki fragments purified from these strains do not exhibit the periodicity characteristic of a proficient replication-coupled nucleosome assembly pathway, but rather peak at length above 400 bp (Figure 7e).
evidence: Okazaki fragment analysis shown in Figure 7e.

claim: The integrity of the Cac1 WHD is required for proper nucleosome formation on the lagging strand during DNA replication.
source: The clear difference in Okazaki fragment formation between the WT and the WHD mutations confirms a deficiency in timely and accurate replication-coupled nucleosome assembly in vivo. These experiments show that the integrity of the Cac1 WHD is required for proper nucleosome formation on the lagging strand during DNA replication, fully supporting our model that places this domain at the heart of the CAF-1 nucleosome assembly mechanism (Figure 6).
evidence: Okazaki fragment data shown in Figure 7e supports the proposed mechanism.

claim: Two CAF-1 complexes are needed for the formation of one tetrasome, with each complex contributing a single H3-H4 dimer.
source: Our work reveals that two CAF-1 complexes are needed for the formation of one tetrasome, with each complex contributing a single H3-H4 dimer.
evidence: Conclusion from stoichiometry and assembly experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: The proposed mechanism provides direct evidence for previously proposed models based on in vivo observations.
source: This provides direct evidence for previously proposed models based on in vivo observations (Nakano et al., 2011; Tagami et al., 2004).
evidence: The experimental findings support previously published models.

claim: The WHD remains in close proximity to H3-H4 on CAF-1.
source: Together, these findings suggest that the WHD remains in close proximity to H3-H4 on CAF-1.
evidence: Inferred from cross-linking studies cited from Liu et al., 2016 and Kim et al., 2016.

claim: At least two CAF-1 complexes may simultaneously bind to one PCNA trimer.
source: Our proposed model also demands that two CAF-1 complexes must be located in close proximity to be able to function together in tetrasome assembly. This implies that at least two CAF-1 complexes may simultaneously bind to one PCNA trimer.
evidence: Logical inference from the proposed mechanism requiring two CAF-1 complexes.

claim: A combination of relatively low affinity interactions (WHD•DNA, and H3•H3' in the H3-H4 tetramerization interface) work together to drive (H3-H4)2 tetramer deposition onto DNA.
source: Overall, our data suggest that a combination of relatively low affinity interactions (WHD•DNA, and H3•H3' in the H3-H4 tetramerization interface) work together to drive (H3-H4)2 tetramer deposition onto DNA.
evidence: Summary interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: An inhibitory intramolecular interaction poises CAF-1 for histone binding and deposition.
source: This study describes the mechanism of histone deposition by CAF-1, a reaction that has remained elusive for other histone chaperones. We demonstrate that an inhibitory intramolecular interaction poises CAF-1 for histone binding and deposition.
evidence: Demonstrated through experiments with acidic region mutants shown in Figure 3.

claim: H3-H4 dimer binding to CAF-1 activates the cascade of events required for its deposition by unmasking the Cac1 WHD to bind DNA.
source: H3-H4 dimer binding to CAF-1 activates the cascade of events required for its deposition, by unmasking the Cac1 WHD to bind DNA.
evidence: Demonstrated through EMSA experiments shown in Figure 3d.

claim: This mechanism ensures that only histone-bound CAF-1 complexes are able to participate in the deposition process.
source: This mechanism ensures that only histone-bound CAF-1 complexes are able to participate in the deposition process, thus optimizing the efficiency of tetrasome assembly and excluding inefficient participation of empty CAF-1 complexes.
evidence: Logical inference from the demonstrated histone-dependent activation of WHD.

claim: High affinity histone binding is not sufficient to sustain efficient nucleosome assembly.
source: By mutating the WHD, we uncouple histone binding and deposition, and demonstrate that high affinity histone binding is not sufficient to sustain efficient nucleosome assembly.
evidence: Demonstrated through experiments with WHD mutants that retain histone binding but show reduced assembly activity.

claim: Not all proteins that bind histones (i.e. histone chaperones) are efficient nucleosome assembly factors.
source: This suggests that not all proteins that bind histones (i.e. histone chaperones) are in fact efficient nucleosome assembly factors.
evidence: Inference from the observation that histone binding alone is insufficient for assembly.

claim: Two independently chaperoned H3-H4 dimers are joined at the very last step of the deposition process, when the DNA is in proximity and available for sequestering the histones from CAF-1.
source: Finally, the observation that two CAF-1•H3-H4 complexes associate to form a tetrasome suggests that two independently chaperoned H3-H4 dimers are joined at the very last step of the deposition process, when the DNA is in proximity and available for sequestering the histones from CAF-1.
evidence: Conclusion from the demonstrated mechanism of tetrasome formation.

claim: The proposed mechanism does not exclude the possibility of a semiconservative model for chromatin assembly coupled with DNA replication.
source: While convincing evidence supports the conservative model, where parental (H3-H4)2 are deposited in the same nucleosome following DNA replication (Xu et al., 2010), our proposed mechanism does not exclude the possibility of a semiconservative model for chromatin assembly coupled with DNA replication (Tagami et al., 2004).
evidence: Discussion of implications of the mechanism in relation to published models.

claim: CAF-1 is a histone H3-H4 chaperone composed of three distinct subunits, all of which are conserved from yeast to humans.
source: CAF-1 is a histone H3-H4 chaperone, composed of three distinct subunits, all of which are conserved from yeast (named Cac1, Cac2 and Cac3) to humans (Almouzni and Méchali, 1988; Kaufman et al., 1995, 1997; Smith and Stillman, 1989; Tyler et al., 1999; Verreault et al., 1996).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from multiple published sources.

claim: CAF-1 directly interacts with the replisome via the processivity factor PCNA.
source: CAF-1 directly interacts with the replisome via the processivity factor PCNA (Krawitz et al., 2002; Moggs et al., 2000; Rolef Ben-Shahar et al., 2009; Shibahara and Stillman, 1999; Zhang et al., 2000) and bridges interactions with epigenetic factors (Loyola et al., 2009; Murzina et al., 1999; Quivy et al., 2008).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from multiple published sources.

claim: CAF-1 is indispensable for the maintenance of cell identity and for life in multicellular organisms.
source: The unique role of CAF-1 in integrating chromatin assembly with DNA synthesis and epigenetic signaling makes it indispensable for the maintenance of cell identity and for life in multicellular organisms (Barbieri et al., 2014; Cheloufi et al., 2015; Houlard et al., 2006; Ishiuchi et al., 2015; Nakano et al., 2011; Song et al., 2007).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from multiple published sources.

claim: In yeast, CAF-1 deletion is viable but results in aberrant transcriptional silencing programs and sensitivity to DNA damage.
source: In yeast, CAF-1 deletion is viable but results in aberrant transcriptional silencing programs and sensitivity to DNA damage (Kaufman et al., 1998).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from published source.

claim: Current evidence favors a conservative model for H3-H4 inheritance, where parental (H3-H4)2 tetramers are not split and distributed onto the daughter strands but rather deposited as one unit.
source: Current evidence favors a conservative model for H3-H4 inheritance, where parental (H3-H4)2 tetramers are not split and distributed onto the daughter strands but rather deposited as one unit (Xu et al., 2010), but alternative models have also been proposed (Tagami et al., 2004).
evidence: Summary of published evidence and models.

claim: The estimated dissociation constant for tetramerization of the H3-H4 dimer is considerably weaker than the affinity of H3-H4 for DNA or for histone chaperones.
source: The estimated dissociation constant for tetramerization of the H3-H4 dimer is considerably weaker than the affinity of H3-H4 for DNA or for the histone chaperones (Donham et al., 2011).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from published source.

claim: The length of Okazaki fragments generated during replication depends on proper nucleosome assembly by CAF-1.
source: To specifically demonstrate that the phenotype observed with CAF-1 complex that is mutated in the WHD is due to an aberrant nucleosome assembly function of Cac1 in vivo, we took advantage of the fact that the length of Okazaki fragments generated during replication depends on proper nucleosome assembly by CAF-1 (Smith and Whitehouse, 2012; Yadav and Whitehouse, 2016).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from published sources.
